the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Greek ​as ​**Τροία**. Etymologically ​it ​means ​"Unknown; possibly ‌from ​Τρωός"[^1].

The ​ASCII ‌form *troia* ​survives ‌only because ​the ‌early domain-name ​system ​could not ​carry ​diacritics; it ​is ‌a ​technological compromise, ‌not ​an ancient ‌spelling. ​The Unicode ‌restoration ​**Troía** recovers ‌the ​stress accent ​of ‌the original ‌directly ‌in the ​address ​bar. ‌The original ​carries ​both stress ‌and ​vowel length, ​and ‌exactly one ​historically ‌valid Unicode ​restoration ​exists, which ​places ​the name ‌in ‌Tier ​1.

The ‌letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

​- ‌**t** → ‌**T** ‌— Tau
‌- ​**r** → ‌**r** ​— Rho
​- ​**o** → ‌**o** ​— ​Short omicron
​- ‌**i** → ​**í** ​— Acute ​on ‌iota
- ​**a** ‌→ **a** ​— ‌Short alpha

​The ‌project holds ‌the ​domain ​**troíā.com** (xn--tro-tma4h.com) ​as ​the canonical ‌home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad, Oxford Classical Texts (Monro & Allen); Loeb, 750 BCE.

overview.body:
**Troía** ​(*troia*) — ‌The City ‌That ​Fell Twice ​— belongs ​to ​the Greek ​tradition, where ‌it ​is catalogued ​under the ‌domain ​"City of ‌Priam". The ​name ‌means "Unknown; ​possibly from ​Τρωός"[^1].

​Troíā is ​the city ​that ‌fell once ​and rose ‌forever: ​ten years ‌of siege ​made ‌it the ​template of ‌Western ​war narrative, ​and its ‌survivors ‌— in ‌Roman myth ​— ​sailed west ‌to found ​the ​lineage of ‌Rome itself. ​Every ​empire since ‌has wanted ​to be ‌Troy's ​heir rather ​than its ​conqueror.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ‌the name ‌as ​**Troía** and ‌serves its ​temple ​at [troíā.com](https://xn--tro-tma4h.com). ‌The original ‌carries ‌both stress ‌and vowel ​length, ‌and exactly ​one historically ​valid ​Unicode restoration ‌exists, which ​places ​the name ​in Tier ‌1. ​The plain ​ASCII form ​*troia* ‌survives as ​a modern ‌convenience ​imposed by ‌the early ​domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, not ​the ​fallback, is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

domains.body:
Troíā ​is the ‌city ‌that ​fell once ​and ​rose ​forever: ten ​years ‌of ​siege made ​it ‌the template ​of ‌Western ​war narrative, ‌and ​its ​survivors — ​in ​Roman ​myth — ‌sailed ​west to ‌found ​the ‌lineage of ​Rome ‌itself. ​Every empire ‌since ​has ​wanted to ‌be ‌Troy's heir ‌rather ​than ​its conqueror.[^1]

‌### ​The ​Walls

Built ‌by ​Poseidṓn ​and Apóllōn ‌— ​walls only ‌a ​trick ​could breach.

​### ​The ‌Horse

Odysseus' ‌stratagem: ​the ‌gift that ​is ​a breach, ‌the ‌original ‌Trojan horse.

‌### ​The ‌Ten Years

​The ​Iliad ​covers fifty ‌days; ​the full ​siege ​cycle ‌filled the ​entire ​Epic ​Cycle.

### ‌The ​Exiles

‌Aeneas carries ​his ‌father and ​his ‌gods ‌out of ​the ​fire ​— Troy's ​fall ‌as ‌Rome's first ​chapter.

mythology.body:
The Trojan ​cycle is the largest ‌story the Greeks ‌told: from the ​wedding of Pēleús and ​the Apple of ​Discord to the ​Returns of the heroes, ​it fills eight ‌epics, of which ​the Iliad and Odyssey ​are only the ‌surviving heart.[^1]

### ​The Apple (The Judgment)

‌Eris, uninvited to ​the wedding of ‌Pēleús and Thetis, threw ​a golden apple ​inscribed "for the fairest." ​Zeús delegated the ​verdict to the ​Trojan prince Paris, herding ‌on Mount Ida: ​Hēra offered empire, ‌Athēnā victory, Aphrodítē the ​most beautiful woman ‌in the world. ​He chose the woman ‌— Helen, wife ​of Menelaos — ‌and the war became ​arithmetic.[^2]

### Nine ​Years and a ‌Quarrel (The Siege)

A ‌thousand ships gathered ‌at Aulis; nine years ​raided the Troad ​before the Iliad ‌even begins. The poem's ​subject is a ​quarrel in the ‌tenth year — Agamemnōn's ​seizure of Brisēis, ​Achilleús' withdrawal, and ‌the chain of deaths ​from Pátroklos to ‌Hektōr — yet ​behind it stands the ​city's doom, prophesied ​and accepted by ​every combatant.

### The ‌Last Night (The ‌Horse)

The Odyssey ​and the Aeneid tell ‌the end the ​Iliad never reaches: the ​Achaeans feign departure, ‌leaving a wooden ‌horse as an "offering ‌to Athēnā." The ‌priest Laokoōn warns ​against it and is ‌destroyed by sea-serpents; ​the prophetess Kassandra ​is disbelieved, as always. ​At night the ‌hidden warriors open ​the Scaean Gate, and ​Troíā burns in ​a single night ‌after ten years of ​failure.

### The ​Dispersal (The Survivors)

Greek ​myth disperses the ‌Trojans across the ​map: Aeneas to Italy ‌in the Roman ​telling, Antēnor to ‌the Adriatic, Hektor's son ​— in the ‌minority tradition — ‌restored in a new ​Troy. The vanquished ​city thus colonizes ​the imagination of its ​conquerors: to be ‌Troianos, "of Troy," ‌becomes, paradoxically, a title ​of glory.

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is ​**/troí.aː/** — ​Attic ​Greek.[^1]

‌For ​the modern ​speaker, ‌the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: TROY-ah, ‌with ​the ​stress ​on the ​final ​syllable ‌and ​a long ‌ā.

​Kindred ‌and ​historical forms ‌of ​the ‌name:

​- **Greek** ​— ‌Τροία
‌- ‌**Latin** ​— Troia
​- ‌**Hittite** ​— ​Wilusa
- ‌**Owned ​form** ​— ‌Troíā

Greek ​Τροία ‌bears ​the ​stress on ​the ​final ‌syllable ‌with a ​long ‌diphthongal ​ending ​— ‌Troíā — ‌and ‌Latin ‌Troia ​keeps both ‌the ​vowels ​and ​the fame. ‌The ​form ​was ​already a ‌place-name ​before ​it ​was a ‌story: ​Hittite ‌records ​call ‌the land ​Wilusa, ‌which ‌most ​scholars now ​connect ​to ​(W)ilios, ‌Troy's other ‌Greek ​name.

meditation.body:
Troíā is ​the city that ‌teaches what walls ‌cannot do. Gods ​built hers; ​a story breached ​them. Every culture ​that has traced ​its ancestry to ‌her fall has ​understood the lesson: ​the defeated city ‌outlived all its ​conquerors because ‌it alone became ​a story that ‌everyone, including its ​enemies, needed to ​tell.

Her deepest ​lesson is the ​one the victors ​learned first: that ‌a story ​is stronger than ‌a wall. The ​Greeks won the ‌war and spent ​three thousand years ‌inside the city's ​aftermath — and ‌Rome, wiser than ​all of ​them, simply claimed ‌to be her. ‌Every culture since ‌has faced the ​same choice at ​her gate: to ‌besiege the past, ​or to inherit ​it.

The ‌Hittite letter and ​the burned layer ​do not prove ‌the Iliad — ​nothing could — ‌but they do ​the more valuable ​thing: they ​give the song ​an address. Every ‌retelling since has ‌been a kind ​of excavation, brushing ‌the myth to ​find the memory ​underneath, and every ‌excavator has ‌found what Schliemann ‌found: that a ‌story told long ​enough and loved ‌enough becomes true ​in the only ​way that finally ​matters — people ‌build on ​it.

Every autumn ​the plain floods ​a little, as ‌the Scamander remembers ​its old bed, ​and the mound ​stands in the ‌water-meadow like the ​ship of ‌the story it ​carries — nine ‌cities deep, one ​name, and still ‌unsinkable.

And the ‌plain is quiet ​now, the way ​famous battlefields are ​— which ​is its own ‌testimony: the war ‌ended, the song ​did not.[^1]
